items.body:
Version bump and changelog for the corrected evaluation instrument merged in #17.

## Why major

`SFRR` measures something different now. Under corrected scoring it falls
8.8–17.6pp on **all ten** reference baselines and the between-baseline ordering
does not survive. Because the artifact share differs per system, **no constant
correction exists** — 1.x numbers need re-deriving, not rescaling. A minor bump
would imply a comparability that isn't there.

The codebase already referred to `v2.0` throughout.

## Verified from the built wheel

Installed into a clean venv to confirm the corrected behavior actually ships,
rather than testing the source tree:

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `"HP"` inside "PHP" | `False` |
| `"100"` inside "1000" | `False` |
| `"Right now, …"` extracted as | `yes` (was `no`) |
| `"budget"` admissible as forbidden phrase | `False` |
| judge resolution | `('openai', 'gpt-4o-mini')` |
| counterfactual axes shipped | 7 |
| CLI `--version` | `2.0.0` |

sdist scanned: no secrets, no results bloat, only `.env.example`.

## Changelog

Leads with **"Do not compare 1.x results to 2.x results"** and the migration
snippet before any feature list. The people most affected are those holding
published 1.x numbers, and they need to know those require re-deriving.

## Not done here

Nothing is published to PyPI. No credentials are present in the environment, and
a PyPI version number is permanent — 2.0.0 can be yanked but never reused. Upload
should follow this merge so the artifact traces to a commit on `main`.

items.title: Push corrected score to Zoho + webhook on manual-review resolve
items.body:
## Summary

Resolving a `manual_review` checkpoint recomputed the parent journey/call overall score in the DB but never re-pushed it downstream. So after a reviewer's final pass/fail verdict, **Zoho (and any outbound webhook subscribers) kept the AI's provisional score and drifted** from the corrected result. This is exactly the case that most needs to reach the CRM, since low-confidence consent gates are the items routed to manual review in the first place.

## What changed

- **New `packages/api/src/services/score-writeback.ts`** — rebuilds the `journey.scored` / `call.scored` payload from persisted DB state and fires the same two downstream side effects the scoring jobs do: the outbound webhook (`deliverCallScored`) and the Zoho write-back (`pushJourneyScored` / `pushCallScored`). Best-effort, never throws. The journey builder replicates the scoring job's exact wrap-up-agent selection so QA attribution/owner stay consistent.
- **`packages/api/src/routes/review.ts`** — the resolve helpers now return the parent id, and the handler re-pushes **after** the transaction commits (so a rolled-back score is never pushed).

## Why not re-run the scoring job

Deliberately does **not** re-enqueue `score-journey` (the re-score button's path): that would spend LLM tokens and re-derive the item back to `manual_review`, overwriting the human verdict. The re-push carries the freshly recomputed score from the DB instead.

## Verification

- `tsc --noEmit` on `packages/api`: clean
- Full api test suite: 40/40 pass

items.title: Fix #839: surface network failures when sending a corrected score
items.body:
Closes #839.

## The bug

`CorrectionEntry` derived its inline alert as:

```ts
const apiError = proposeMutation.error instanceof ApiError ? proposeMutation.error : null;
```

`useProposeResult` runs with `networkMode: 'always'`, so submitting a correction while offline **does** fire the POST, and `fetch` rejects at the transport level with a plain `TypeError` — never an `ApiError`. So `apiError` is `null`. With a valid decided board `boardHint` is `null` too, so *neither* `role="alert"` paragraph rendered. The button showed "Sending…", re-enabled, and the user got **zero feedback** that the send had failed.

## The fix

Add a `networkError` branch for non-`ApiError` rejections, rendered with the existing inline-error pattern:

> Couldn't send your corrected score — check your connection and try again.

It is mutually exclusive with `apiError` by construction (an error is one or the other), so the 409 "This proposal has moved on…" copy is untouched.

## Design decisions

- **Error-driven, not a `navigator.onLine` pre-check.** An at-submit check misses mid-flight drops and DNS failures, and `navigator.onLine` reports `true` with no real connectivity. Reacting to the rejection catches every case.
- **No defer-to-scratchpad**, unlike `score-entry.tsx`. A score is safe to queue; silently queuing a *negotiation correction* would make the user believe it sent. Surfacing the failure is correct.
- **The button re-enable is left alone** — that behaviour is right, it permits a retry.

## On the test

The regression test rejects the POST at the transport level (`HttpResponse.error()`), on a valid decided board so `boardHint` is `null` — the exact state where the old code rendered nothing.

It waits for the mutation to *settle* (a signal present in both the fixed and broken states) and then asserts the alert **synchronously**. This matters: this suite sets `asyncUtilTimeout: 5000` and no `testTimeout` override, so a naive `waitFor` on the alert reds with a bare `Test timed out in 5000ms` — indistinguishable from a hang, and proof of nothing. As written, deleting the branch reds in ~400ms with `unable to find an accessible element with the role "alert"`.

Verified by removing the JSX branch and re-running: **1 failed / 10 passed**, assertion error at the `getByRole("alert")` line. Restored: **16 passed**.

## Verification

- `vitest run` (full web-client suite) — **1228 passed, 183 files**
- `tsc -b` — clean
- `npm run lint` — 0 errors
- No API/schema change: `schema.d.ts` untouched, no `regen-api-types`, no `e2e/` stub updates needed.

items.title: feat: score corrected transcripts and republish WER
items.body:
## Context

Every published number in this repository measures raw ASR output or
diarization. Nothing measures the correction lane — the lane that is the
product's actual review path: the operator supplies a terminology list and the
model repairs the transcript against it, with no human editing pass. There was
no way to answer "did correction help, and did it break anything".

Building that measurement surfaced a metric bug that had to be fixed first, and
fixing it moves two published numbers.

**The normalization bug.** `docs/contracts/scoring.md` declares punctuation
*removal*; `metrics.py` replaced punctuation with *spaces*. Reference `dont` vs
hypothesis `don't` therefore normalized to `dont` vs `don t` — one substitution
plus one insertion, WER 2.0 instead of 0. Correction routinely rewrites
punctuation, so scoring corrected text under the old normalizer would count
punctuation edits as word errors. The contract was right; the code was wrong.

**Republication (maintainer-approved 2026-08-11).** Fixing it changes WER only —
CER is mathematically invariant because character scoring strips all whitespace
after normalization:

| Published value | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Korean VibeVoice WER | 0.128 | 0.141 |
| Italian MOSS WER | 0.081 | 0.085 |
| All CER values | unchanged | unchanged |

Term recall, omissions, and backchannel 7/7 do not move.

## Changes

- **`metrics.py`** deletes punctuation instead of replacing it with spaces, per
  the declared contract. Apostrophe (ASCII and typographic), hyphen, NFKC,
  case, whitespace, and Italian-diacritic behavior are pinned by tests.
- **`score.py`** opens its output exclusive-create; an existing scores artifact
  is preserved instead of truncated (judgment rule 3: artifacts are
  create-only).
- **Republication in the same change**: `benchmarks/published-results.json`
  (with fresh artifact SHA-256 provenance), all ten READMEs, the four generated
  figures, both historical verdict docs, the app profile resource and the app
  test that pins those values, and a new `D36 [maintainer]` decision record in
  `PROJECT.md`.
- **`score_corrected.py`** (new): scores a correction run's raw and corrected
  output against one reference. Before trusting any number it verifies the
  correction respected the contract — segment count, speakers, timestamps,
  source, language, confidence all unchanged — and rejects with the offending
  segment and field named. Reports per-metric directional deltas,
  applied-vs-review counts, and correction-safety classification.
- **Correction-safety counting**: an applied change is evaluated only when
  exactly one reference segment has the identical time interval; raw and
  corrected CER/WER edit counts are then compared Pareto-style (`closer`,
  `further`, `mixed`, `unchanged`, plus `correct_to_incorrect` when a correct
  segment was rewritten wrong). If any applied change cannot be aligned,
  `correction_made_worse_count` is `null` rather than a misleading zero, with
  the observed count and unevaluated list alongside.
- **`compare_correction_paths.py`** (new): the four-state harness — no-glossary
  ASR, decode-time glossary ASR, each corrected — emitting one create-only
  verdict JSON with the three deltas that matter: decode-time injection gain,
  correction gain, correction gain without decode-time injection. Thresholds
  live in a versioned JSON file; every value is deliberately `null` and the
  verdict stays `passed: null` until the maintainer sets standards.

## Validation

- Scoring suite: **69/69** (baseline before the change: 49/49, zero failures).
- Contract checker: all three schemas pass.
- README checker: all ten files match the declaration.
- Figure suite: 6/6 after regenerating the four SVGs.
- `swift build` passes; the app test target passes **45 tests in 7 suites**
  after updating the two pinned WER values.
- Red-then-green evidence recorded for the normalizer fix (4 failures before),
  the corrected scorer, and the harness.
- A synthetic four-state demonstration produces the expected deltas, including
  one deliberate `correct_to_incorrect` regression caught by the safety count.

Not verified: a live correction turn against a real model — the harness
consumes completed run directories and this host has no pinned model caches.
The fixture demonstration covers the tooling, not model behavior.

## Notes for review

- `Tests/MaccheroniAppTests/AppShellTests.swift` is also touched by #9 in a
  different region; whichever merges second rebases trivially.
- A follow-up contract doc should specify the corrected-score JSON shape and
  the four-state verdict semantics; flagged in the report rather than edited,
  since `docs/contracts/` changes deserve their own review.
- The threshold placeholders in
  `benchmarks/scripts/scoring/correction-comparison-thresholds.json` are yours
  to set; the harness reports `not_configured` until then.

Add trainable paired-score transcription vertical slice
items.body:
### Motivation
- The existing v0.1 pipeline is deterministic and cannot learn from paired performance/score examples or produce reproducible trainable artifacts, and it lacks an authoritative typed score model and paired-example alignment storage. 
- To enable reproducible supervised learning and human-in-the-loop corrections we need content-addressed paired-example ingestion, a typed rational-score representation, explicit performance↔score alignment, and a compact trainable reranker that integrates with the deterministic pipeline. 
- The change implements a constrained first vertical slice that preserves provenance and evidence while exposing clear interfaces for future hierarchical inference and improved candidate generation.

### Description
- Introduces a typed, exact-rational internal Score model and deterministic MusicXML/.mxl normalization and serialization (`src/midiscore/representation/score.py`, `src/midiscore/representation/__init__.py`).
- Adds content-addressed paired-dataset storage with SHA-256 object copy, stable example IDs, required license/provenance fields, normalized-score artifacts, alignment artifacts, validation, and piece-grouped split logic (`src/midiscore/dataset/storage.py`, `src/midiscore/dataset/__init__.py`).
- Implements a monotonic dynamic-programming alignment that yields explicit `matched|ambiguous|insertion|deletion` records with timing residuals and confidences (`src/midiscore/dataset/alignment.py`).
- Adds a compact trainable candidate reranker baseline (pairwise linear ranker) with deterministic training and JSON checkpointing, plus application code to apply a checkpoint at inference time (`src/midiscore/models_baseline.py`).
- Adds feedback import and pairwise-preference artifacts that convert corrected MusicXML into typed, atomic corrections suitable for later training (`src/midiscore/feedback_learning.py`).
- Adds evaluation metrics and machine-readable/Markdown report generation for alignment and typed-score comparisons (`src/midiscore/evaluation.py`).
- Extends the CLI with dataset management (`dataset init/add/validate/list/split`), `train`, `evaluate`, `feedback import-corrected-score` and `feedback prefer`, and adds `--engine` (`heuristic|learned|hybrid`) and `--checkpoint` controls to `transcribe` (`src/midiscore/cli.py`, `src/midiscore/application.py`).
- Includes documentation and a guide (`docs/trainable-system.md`) and a test suite that exercises ingestion, normalization round-trip, alignment, training on the tiny fixture, hybrid inference, evaluation reporting, and corrected-score import (`tests/test_learning_vertical_slice.py`).
- Example reproduce commands (CLI): `midiscore dataset init DATASET_DIR`, `midiscore dataset add --dataset DATASET_DIR --midi performance.mid --score reference.musicxml --license LICENSE --provenance PROVENANCE`, `midiscore train --dataset DATASET_DIR --output-dir models/run-001 --seed 1729`, `midiscore transcribe INPUT.mid --engine hybrid --checkpoint models/run-001/best.ckpt --output-dir run`, `midiscore evaluate --dataset DATASET_DIR --checkpoint models/run-001/best.ckpt --split test --output-dir evaluations/run-001`, and `midiscore feedback import-corrected-score run --corrected-score corrected.musicxml --author alice`.

### Testing
- Static and quality gates: `ruff check .`, `ruff format --check .`, and `mypy src` all passed in the CI-like run. 
- Unit and integration tests: `pytest -q` — all tests passed (10 passed), including the new vertical-slice integration test which runs: demo MIDI generation → transcribe → dataset init/add/validate → split → train → checkpointed hybrid inference → evaluate → import-corrected-score.
- Manual end-to-end CLI smoke: exercised via `python -m midiscore` (demo → transcribe → dataset add → train → hybrid transcribe → evaluate → feedback import) and produced evaluation metrics and feedback artifacts as JSON/Markdown.
- Package build step: `python -m build` was not completed in this environment because installing the `build` dependency was blocked by package-index/network restrictions; this is an environment limitation, not a source/test failure. 
- Determinism and limitations: checkpoints and training record seeds/Git SHA/dependency versions and are deterministic under fixed seeds; the PR does not claim the learned reranker yet outperforms the legacy heuristic baseline and documents current functional limitations (partwise-only MusicXML support, monotonic DP alignment rather than hierarchical onset-group/local-tempo models, ranker limited to onset/duration subdivision candidates, WAV retained as metadata only).

items.title: Add score_locked override so the sync stops clobbering a manually-corrected score
items.body:
Follow-up to #58, which merged before this commit was pushed, so the `score_locked`
mechanism never reached `main`.

## Context

Spain vs Saudi Arabia (World Cup 2026): the official result is **4-0**, but the football-data.org feed returns `fullTime 5-0` and never corrects it. The sync re-applied 5-0 on every tick, so points were computed on a wrong score, with no way to fix it.

## Changes

- Migration adding `score_locked BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE` on `matches`.
- When the flag is `true`, the sync keeps the manually-set `home_score` / `away_score` / `status` and ignores the feed's outcome for that match, while still refreshing the other fields.

## Prod correction procedure (after deploy)

```sql
UPDATE matches SET home_score = 4, away_score = 0, score_locked = TRUE WHERE id = 537371;
```
Points recompute on the next tick (`recompute_all` is idempotent) and players receive a "🚫 Goal disallowed: Spain 4-0 Saudi Arabia" push.

items.title: Align worked-example verdict with the non-compensable principle
items.body:
## Why

The closing line of the worked example read *"The average does not decide the assignment. The failed critical requirement does."* It's a sound general AAF principle, but it is **not what this specific example proves**: with the corrected scores, Agent B's average (4.2) is actually *higher* than Agent A's (4.0), so here the average and the classification agree. A careful reader would notice the example doesn't support that sentence.

## Change

Replace the verdict with a statement the example genuinely demonstrates, using the same *non-compensable* language as the AAF specification and the public post:

> A failed critical requirement **cannot be compensated for by strength elsewhere.**

Agent A is stronger than Agent B in four of five dimensions yet still classifies as A1 — a direct proof of non-compensability.

## Result

One consistent message across the specification, the site, the embedded image and the LinkedIn post. Re-rendered in Chromium (1320px) to confirm the line displays correctly with its emphasis.

## Summary
`levantemodels::score_irt()` had a column-order bug (mirt::fscores() matches `response.pattern` columns to model items by position, not name). It was fixed upstream in [levantemodels#9](https://github.com/levante-framework/levantemodels/pull/9), so `levantemodels:::score_irt()` no longer reproduces the bug — several notebooks here called it expecting buggy output, which made their buggy-vs-corrected comparisons stale/wrong.

- `common.R`: removed `score_with_method()` (a local reimplementation of `score_irt()`'s internals, parameterized by fscores method — risked drifting from the package's own fix). Replaced with:
  - `score_task_irt()` — thin plumbing wrapper (spec lookup, filter, recode) that delegates all scoring to `levantemodels::score_irt()`
  - `score_irt_buggy()` — `score_irt()`'s current logic with the column-reorder step removed, to reproduce the pre-fix behavior for historical comparison
- `tasks/math_eap_vs_ml.qmd`, `tasks/vocab.qmd`, `tasks/stories_tom.qmd`: "corrected"/"fixed" scores now come from `levantemodels::score_irt()` directly; "buggy" scores come from `score_irt_buggy()`

**Depends on** [levante-framework/levantemodels#23](https://github.com/levante-framework/levantemodels/pull/23), which adds the `method=` argument to `score_irt()` that `score_task_irt()` and the notebooks' EAP/ML comparisons rely on. Until #23 merges and this repo's `levantemodels` install/renv lock is bumped, these notebooks won't render (method= argument doesn't exist yet in the installed package).

items.title: feat(factor-panel): real equity panel + HAC-corrected, vectorized scoring
items.body:
The factor stack (F1–F4, H1, H2) was built and pinned on a **synthetic** panel. This is its first run on **real** equities — shipped together with the two scoring fixes that first run motivated (the combined increment).

## 1. Real panel — the first real exploration is a conservative null

`factor_panel.py` + `factor_universe_prices.csv`: a committed, hand-selected universe of **42 large-cap US equities** (`FACTOR_UNIVERSE`), split/dividend-adjusted daily closes from yfinance assembled into a dates×tickers panel (**42 × 2514 days, 2016–2026, zero gaps**). The CSV is committed like the repo's other free price CSVs (1.95MB; not premium option-chain data).

**The result: 0 of 63 grammar factors survive the e-LOND bar on US large-caps; all 63 type coherently (35 trend / 28 lowvol).** The machinery scores, types, and FDR-controls correctly on real data and finds no edge. EXPLORATORY — promotion CLOSED, with **survivorship + 1-day-horizon + frozen-snapshot caveats stated loudly** ([docs/factor_real_panel.md](docs/factor_real_panel.md)). `make_factor_backend` stamps each row's `end` with the panel's actual last date.

## 2. HAC correction — the field name is now accurate

`factor_backend._newey_west_t`: the factor IC t-stat is now **Newey-West HAC-corrected** for the IC series' autocorrelation (adjacent days share most of the cross-section), mirroring `cc_backtest.compute_statistics`' Bartlett-weighted convention. So the shared honest-core field `t_stat_newey_west` is now **literally accurate** for factors (no misnomer, no disclosure caveat). 0/63 still survive under the proper t (max |t_nw| = 1.52).

## 3. Vectorization — ~60× faster

`information_coefficient` + `long_short_returns` replaced their per-date Python loops with rank-based vectorized pandas/numpy, **verified `allclose` 1e-12** against the originals (behavior-preserving). The real-panel full search drops from **~2-3 min to ~2s**; the factor test suite from ~2-3 min to ~10s. Fast enough that the dataset-gated test now pins the **full 0/63 headline directly**, not a 6-factor proxy.

## Review

Two adversarial agents. The correctness agent found **no bugs** — the NW mirrors the option reference exactly, the vectorization is mathematically equivalent (mask/rank/demean/portfolio logic preserved), the HAC symmetry property preserves `rev == -mom`, and there's no behavior regression (IC values unchanged, foil-paper gate + e-LOND wiring intact). The honesty agent confirmed the docs are accurate after the changes; its should-fixes are applied (and I used the speedup to upgrade the test rather than just patch text). 81 factor tests pass in 10s, ruff clean.

A large PR (data + a stat change + a perf refactor + re-pins) — the combined path, chosen deliberately so the real panel arrives with scoring already accurate and fast, no ship-then-supersede churn.

## Summary

This PR implements the calibration recommendations from the July 21 threshold audit, fixing a critical bug in Stage 6 and introducing a new precision lever in Stage 5. The changes are backed by a comprehensive backfill analysis of 567 labelled webpage candidates with ground-truth LLM verdicts.

## Key Changes

### Stage 6: Remove double-sigmoid bug
- **Removed** the `_sigmoid()` function and its application in `_score_pair()` 
- The cross-encoder model already returns a probability in [0, 1] via its built-in sigmoid activation; applying a second sigmoid was compressing the entire score range into [0.5, 0.731], destroying the gate's discriminative power
- **Fixed behavior**: `_score_pair()` now returns the model's probability directly, clamped to [0, 1]
- This fix alone (with no threshold change) converts Stage 6 from a no-op into a working gate: the unchanged `threshold: 0.60` now rejects 8% of false positives at 100% recall (was 0%)
- Updated all Stage 6 tests to reflect the corrected scoring model

### Stage 5: Implement bi-encoder max-chunk floor
- Added new config parameter `max_chunk_floor` (default: null/disabled for backwards compatibility)
- The floor is applied as an absolute veto on top of the existing OR-logic (high-threshold path OR low-medium path)
- Set to **0.63** in `tripwire_config.yaml` based on calibration data: every known true positive scored ≥ 0.666, providing a 0.036 safety margin
- Effect: removes ~24% of false-positive LLM calls (138 of 546 noise pages) while retaining 100% recall on the labelled set
- Added comprehensive tests for floor enforcement and interaction with existing pass paths

items.title: chore(mutation): publish the measured score, 99.59%
items.body:
## Why this is a second PR

#37 merged before the mutation run finished, so `main` carries the directives and the gate while the README still publishes **95.74%** — the score from before ten equivalents stopped being counted as mutants the suite failed to kill. The published number now understates the package.

## The measurement

`pnpm mutation`, Stryker 9, `break: 95`:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mutation score | 95.74% | **99.59%** |
| Killed | 246 | 240 |
| Survived | 11 | **1** |

No test changed and no production logic changed. The move is entirely the ten equivalents leaving the denominator.

## The one that stays counted

`source-mapping.ts` — the acronym regex, `[A-Z]+` → `[A-Z]`. The mutation is equivalent: the underscore's position is fixed by the following `[A-Z][a-z]` boundary, which both variants locate identically.

It is **not** silenced, and that was settled by measuring rather than reasoning. With `// Stryker disable next-line Regex` on the line above, the run still reported it surviving — a directive does not attach to a `.replace()` inside a method chain. The only way to silence it would be a block directive spanning the neighbouring `.replace()`, whose own regex mutants the suite *does* kill, and a killable mutant is never disabled to raise a number.

So the ineffective directive is replaced by a plain comment that argues the equivalence and states why it is not a directive, and the mutant stays in the score. That is the escape hatch the shared policy already describes: where the source cannot carry the reason, the report carries it and the mutant stays counted.

## Verification

`typecheck`, `lint`, `check:mutants`, `check:published` pass locally; the run itself is the evidence for the number.

Released as **1.0.3** — the README and its badge ship inside the package, so a corrected score that stays on `main` leaves the npm page understating it.

items.title: feat(benchmark): leaderboard artifacts as spec-conformant EvalScoreRecords (#9265)
items.body:
> **Stacked** on #9600 (stack #9601): #9595 → #9598 → #9599 → #9600 → this.

## What

#9216 requirement 5 is explicit that leaderboard artifacts are **exactly** the eval-interface's consumable score records — no parallel format. So this emits `EvalScoreRecord`s with `workUnit.kind === "benchmark_run"` through the same `contentDigest` path the `outcome_confirmed_precision` records already use, and derives the board from those records and **nothing else**.

That last point is the structural one: there is no second query path from the scorer to the board. A number on the leaderboard is, by construction, a field of a record a third party can fetch, re-derive and digest-verify — so the published board and the consumable feed cannot disagree, because they're the same data read twice.

## Two policies enforced here rather than left to a caller's discipline

**Held-out cadence (#9263 decision 2).** The emitter is the last point before a number becomes public, so it's where cadence is enforced. A held-out record is simply **not built** while the window is open — not built-and-filtered, not built-with-a-flag — so there is no in-memory held-out record for a downstream bug to serialize. The regression test probes this with the would-be record's own **digest**, a 64-hex value unique to that exact content, because my first attempt used the held-out precision as the probe and it was `0` — a substring of almost any JSON, so it passed for the wrong reason.

**Trust tier from the actual execution.** `attested` requires a real envelope; absent one the tier is `reproducible`, never optimistically upgraded. The record type's discriminated union already makes "attested without an envelope" unrepresentable, and the tier sits inside the digest preimage, so a tier claim can't be edited after issuance (asserted: the two tiers produce different digests for otherwise-identical content).

## Score mapping and ranking

The score block maps the multi-class report onto the spec's fixed fields without inventing any: `precision`/`recall` are #9262's **macro** headline, `decided`/`abstained`/`coverage` come from the report's own coverage block, and `confirmed` is the count of decided units the agent got right. Ranking is macro precision descending with **null last** (unmeasurable is not zero, and sorting it as 0 would invent a claim), ties broken by coverage descending then by the earlier `issuedAt`. Immutability is respected rather than worked around: several records for one subject resolve to the latest `issuedAt`, because a corrected score is a new record, never a mutation.

## Tests (14, 100% of branches)

Spec conformance including an exact top-level key set (no extra fields); full commitments block with no placeholders; the score mapping; the decided-nothing null arms; both trust tiers with distinct digests; the not-built-while-open regression; publication at close and on a cadence boundary but not a day either side; the ranking comparator across every arm (null-vs-null falling through to coverage, the `?? -1` fallback from both argument positions, the earlier-claim tiebreak, order-independence); the corrected-score regression; cross-benchmark and cross-kind exclusion; and the empty set.

Also registers the module in `check-dead-source-files`' staged-ahead allowlist — the emitter lands before its serving route (#9216's endpoint sub-issue) and before #9264 supplies the envelopes its `attested` tier consumes, so the checker's flag was correct and the entry names both, as the checker itself instructs.

Closes #9265

items.title: feat(scoring): floor-corrected partial credit instead of a binary reward
items.body:
<!-- ccr-projects-attribution -->
_Requested by **Hugh** via a Claude Code Project_

**This is the top of the stack and the only layer that changes the reward scale. It can be held back indefinitely without blocking anything below it.** Read the downsides section before the rest — they are real, and a reviewer has to weigh them, not just skim them.

## Before / After

**Before.** The reward is binary. `tests/test.sh` runs pytest and writes `1` or `0` from its exit code. A model that gets most of the way through a task scores the same as one that does nothing at all, and every sweep throws away the per-test detail pytest already recorded.

**After.** The reward is a fraction of the tests that actually carry signal:

```
credit = (passed tests not in the floor) / (tests not in the floor)
```

The **floor** is the set of test *names* that pass against the untouched task image, with no agent having run — measured per task, never written by hand. A full pass still writes the literal byte `1`. A do-nothing agent scores exactly `0`. In between, a partially solved task now reports how much was solved.

**Why the floor is not optional.** On this branch **22 of the 53 tasks pass at least one test with no agent**, and `undo_mistaken_rebase` passes **4 of its 6** — by design, because that task's correct end state *is* the bootstrap state and only the operation log tells a real solve apart. A naive `passed / tests` would pay a do-nothing agent 0.667 there, 0.5 on six other tasks, and 0.16 per task averaged across the benchmark: roughly eight tasks' worth of score handed out for nothing. `ROADMAP.md` records the opposite as the acceptance criterion for that very task ("nop agent scores 0.0, real agent 1.0").

**Why the floor is a set of names and not a count.** Subtracting the floor *count* reports real progress as nothing. On `undo_mistaken_rebase` an agent that performs the rebase but never undoes it passes 3 of 6 against a floor of 4, so `(passed - floor) / (tests - floor)` scores it **0**. By name, 1 of the 2 *scored* tests passed, and it earns **0.500000** — measured in a container, output below. Name-based scoring also makes the nop-agent zero **structural rather than arithmetic**: the only tests a nop agent passes are the floored ones, so its numerator is empty by construction, on every task, whatever the counts happen to be.

## Honest downsides

**It silently disables harbor's pass@k.** `harbor/utils/pass_at_k.py` bails on any reward that is not exactly 0 or 1, and `harbor/cli/jobs.py` then simply omits the columns **with no warning**. `0.0` and `1.0` are fine — this scheme writes literal `1` for a pass and literal `0` for a no-credit trial, so a sweep in which every trial fully passes or fully fails still prints pass@k. The moment one model lands in between, that model's pass@k vanishes while other models keep theirs. That asymmetry is worse than losing the metric outright, because the columns appear and disappear depending on the data. Emitting a second, strict reward key does not rescue it either — harbor bails on more than one key first. `ROADMAP.md` asks for pass@5 on the A/B harness; that metric would have to be computed outside harbor from now on, cheaply as `reward >= 1.0` in `scripts/check_run_results.py`, and that work is **not** in this PR.

**After flooring, 11 tasks still have a single scorable test and remain effectively 0/1.** They are `bookmark_delete`, `bookmark_rename`, `describe_commit`, `diffedit_interactive`, `duplicate_commit`, `git_import`, `history_rewriting`, `rebase_destination`, `restore_specific_revision`, `squash_commits`, `stacking_changes`. 21 more have exactly two scored tests, i.e. one intermediate step. Across the benchmark 30 of 161 tests are floored, leaving 131 scored. Flooring eats hardest into the tasks with the most tests: `undo_mistaken_rebase` drops from 6 tests to 2 scored. So half the benchmark gains at most one step of resolution, which is consistent with `ROADMAP.md` ranking partial credit last of three headroom moves.

**Any aggregate mean reward is a NEW scale with no back-comparison to the existing baselines.** On this scale a model that fails every task by a little scores above 0 where the old scale said 0. The `53/53`, `53/53` and `49/53` rows in `ROADMAP.md` are **not** comparable to a new mean. What *is* comparable is the strict pass count, because a full pass still writes literal `1` and every strict consumer keeps working unchanged and keeps meaning the same thing: `scripts/check_run_results.py` (`reward >= 1.0`), `site/scripts/compute-tasks.ts` (`reward === 1.0`), `harbor/analyze/analyzer.py` (`== 1.0`). Report both, label them, and never put a mean reward next to a historical `49/53` without saying which is which.

**A floored test is, by definition, a test carrying no signal.** The floor file is a list of tests that cannot distinguish a solve from an untouched repository. Flooring them is the right *scoring* behaviour and it is what this PR does, but it should not be read as normal. Most of the 22 are legitimate preservation guards, deliberately written to hold in the bootstrap state — "the file must still be on disk", "the other commits must not be destroyed", "no divergence", "`app.py` must NOT be restored" — and those should keep failing loudly on a destructive agent even though they can never earn credit. **Three of them were not guards but simply weak tests, and they were repaired in the layer immediately below this one rather than floored.** Their repair shows up here as measured numbers: `rebase_branch` 2/3 floored becomes 1/3, `absorb_changes` 1/3 becomes 0/3, `status_ignored` 2/4 becomes 1/4. Fixing a weak test is strictly better than flooring it, and flooring freezes a weak verifier in place; the floor is the mitigation, not the answer.

**The cost of scoring by name: a broken guard test is not charged for.** Floored tests are out of the denominator, so failing them cannot reduce the fraction — and the floored tests are exactly the preservation guards. An agent that does half the work and destroys something scores the same as one that does half the work cleanly. Three things blunt this, none of them a fix: credit is capped strictly below 1 whenever pytest exits non-zero, so a broken guard can never read as a solve; the reason line names every floored test that failed, visible in the `0.500000` run below; and `ctrf.json` still records every failure per test. If charging for guards is wanted, the honest way is an explicit rule — any failing floored test forces reward 0 — not going back to subtracting counts, which mis-scores real progress as nothing.

**Every floor is a measurement, so it needs the containers.** The `--check` in the per-task CI job is nearly free, because it reuses the `ctrf.json` the vacuity step already produced. A local regeneration is a 53-image build. Floors are also tied to the pinned jj version: a jj bump can move a floor, and the first sign will be a red `--check` rather than an explanation.

**The harbor CLI's reward histogram gets noisy.** `harbor/models/job/result.py` buckets rewards by exact value, so the summary prints one row per distinct fraction instead of two rows. The at-a-glance "how many passed" read from that summary is gone; use `scripts/check_run_results.py`, which still counts strictly.

**Sequencing.** This changes the reward scale. Landing it before the re-baseline means the new baseline is the only one on the new scale; landing it after means owning two scales. Either way the strict pass count survives as the comparable number — and if the re-baseline still shows frontier models at 53/53, the honest conclusion is `ROADMAP.md`'s: the benchmark needs harder tasks, not a finer scale on the ones it has.

## How

**`tests/test.sh`, one file, byte-identical in all 53 tasks.** It scores from the per-test `name` and `status` entries in `/logs/verifier/ctrf.json`, which `pytest --ctrf` already writes on every trial; the pytest invocation itself is unchanged. The scoring key is the test function name — the part after the last `::` — because CTRF records pytest's rootdir-relative nodeid and the path part can move if the verifier is ever invoked from elsewhere, while the function name cannot. The script checks those names are unique rather than assuming it. Pure bash plus the Python standard library; no pip, no network.

**The floor file rides in `tests/`.** `tasks/TASK/tests/vacuity_floor.json` sits in the very directory harbor copies to `/tests`, which is exactly what lets `test.sh` stay byte-identical across all 53 — `scripts/lint_tasks.py` still enforces that by sha256, and it is verified below straight out of the commit. The file records `task`, `tests`, `floor`, `passes_without_agent` and `generated_by`. `floor` is redundant with the length of the name list on purpose: `test.sh`, `vacuity_floor.py --check` and `lint_tasks.py` all cross-check the two, so a hand edit to either is caught.

**`scripts/vacuity_floor.py` measures them; nothing hand-writes them.** `--write` builds each task image, runs the verifier against the untouched bootstrap with no network, and records which tests passed. `--check` re-measures and exits non-zero on any disagreement, **comparing name sets** and reporting which names appeared and which disappeared — so a verifier weakened until a *different* test passes on an untouched repo fails the build even though the count did not move. `--task` selects, `--jobs` parallelises, and `--ctrf` scores a report the caller already has, which is the path CI uses so the per-task job never builds an image twice.

**What `test.sh` writes, in every case.** A full pass writes `1`, and no scored test passing writes `0`. Everything else is deliberately conservative:

| situation | reward.txt | classified as |
|---|---|---|
| pytest exit 0 | `1` | PASS |
| some scored tests pass, some tests fail | e.g. `0.500000`, always strictly below 1 | FAIL |
| no scored test passes | `0` | FAIL |
| floor file missing, unparseable, or not a name list | `0` plus a loud reason on stdout | FAIL (strict) |
| floor file stale (its test count differs from the run) | `0` plus a loud reason | FAIL (strict) |
| **floor names a test the run never reported** | `0` plus a loud reason naming it | FAIL (strict) |
| floor covers every test | `0` plus a loud reason | FAIL |
| duplicate or nameless tests in the report | `0`, report moved to `ctrf.json.unscored`, exit 1 | **ERRORED-INFRA** |
| report internally inconsistent | same | **ERRORED-INFRA** |
| pytest never reported a test, or report unreadable | same | **ERRORED-INFRA** |

Two of those rows are worth naming explicitly. The bolded one is the case a count-based sanity check *cannot* catch: a renamed or removed test keeps the count identical while silently shifting the denominator, and `test.sh` refuses to score it. And **a missing or stale floor file does not mean "empty floor"** — it falls back to the strict pre-partial-credit verdict, because assuming an empty floor would silently pay a nop agent on exactly the tasks this scheme exists to protect. Credit is also **capped strictly below 1** whenever pytest exits non-zero: with name-based scoring every scored test can pass while a floored guard fails, and that must never read as a solve to a `>= 1.0` consumer.

The last three rows are the "a crashed verifier must not look like a legitimate 0" requirement. Harbor needs *some* parseable number in `reward.txt` — it raises on an absent or empty file and ignores the script's exit status — so `0` is written, but the unusable report is moved aside rather than deleted, and `scripts/check_run_results.py` already keys `ERRORED-INFRA` off the absence of `verifier/ctrf.json`. A reason lands in `verifier_error.txt`, and `test.sh` exits 1 so CI fails on it too.

**The CI vacuity gate.** The old gate did a **string** compare, `[ "$reward" != "0" ]`, which cannot survive a float reward — an honest zero arriving as `0.0` or `0.000000` would be reported as a vacuous verifier. It is now a numeric comparison, and `scripts/vacuity_floor.py --check` runs in the same step against that very run's `ctrf.json`. `test.sh`'s exit status is captured and diagnosed rather than aborting the step bare. `scripts/vacuity_floor.py` was added both to the workflow's `paths:` filter and to the "shared tooling changed, run every task" escalation.

**`scripts/lint_tasks.py`** gains `tests/vacuity_floor.json` as a required file and a `check_vacuity_floor` that parses it, requires all five keys, checks the task name matches its directory and that `generated_by` names the measuring script, rejects duplicate names, cross-checks `floor` against the names listed, requires `floor` to be below `tests`, requires `tests` to equal the number of `def test_` functions in `test_final_state.py`, and requires every floored name to still be defined there. A separate `check_test_sh_reads_floor` makes reverting `test.sh` to a floor-blind version fail — without it, all 53 copies would still agree with each other and the lint would stay green while 53 floor files sat unread. The inventory now prints the floor distribution and names **every** floored test on every CI run, so a floored test cannot quietly become invisible infrastructure. The byte-identical check is untouched.

## Layer and base

This is **layer 4**, the top of the chain. Base branch: **`claude/hearth-thread-igwt01-vacuous`** (PR #19), which is based on `claude/hearth-thread-igwt01-verifiers` (PR #18), which is based on `claude/hearth-thread-igwt01` (PR #17).

Because this layer changes `scripts/lint_tasks.py` and `.github/workflows/tasks.yml`, CI escalates its matrix to **all 53 tasks** instead of only the tasks touched. ## Why this experiment exists

Your own merged #502 established **rule 53**: there is no decode dispatch residue. A 24-label ledger closes to +0.3 µs/step over 406/406 dispatches, and the entire 592.9 µs "launch/ramp" pool is closed. Nezuko's merged #498 established **rule 55**: all three dominant trio kernels are memory-bandwidth-bound on M4 at 92.2 % of sequential-read peak, with 3.5–50 % free-ALU headroom.

The conclusion is blunt: **the next gain must remove BYTES or restructure attention.** Nezuko has attention. You have bytes.

A full NVFP4 weight-layout and DRAM-traffic audit this round produced the exact per-step byte ledger. Decode streams **≈1.58 GB of weight bytes per token**. Almost all of it is already at 4.13–4.25 bits/weight. **Two families are still at 16 bits/weight:**

| family | bytes/step | bits/weight | share of step |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| layer-0 dense MLP (BF16) | 100,663,296 | 16 | 6.4 % |
| **routers (BF16) — YOURS** | **40,934,400** | **16** | **2.6 %** |

Together **141.6 MB = 9.0 % of step bytes**, worth ~0.64 % of score at the realised ledger price — **61 % of our entire 1.0498 % deficit to the record**. maple-fern is attacking the layer-0 MLP with a different mechanism (deterministic lossless compaction). You are attacking the router with a **certified data-dependent screen**. Whichever technique wins transfers to the other tensor next round.

## The hard constraint: this must be LOSSLESS

`TASK.md:92–94` — the accepted attention-quantization envelope permits group-32 affine INT8 for **Q/K/V/O and per-head `g_proj` only**. **Routers are outside that envelope.** You may not simply store the router in a lower precision.

What you *may* do is compute a **certified screen**: a cheap low-precision pass with a rigorous error bound, plus an **exact re-read** of any expert whose bounded score interval could possibly cross the selection boundary. The output is then **bit-identical to the current router**, and the byte saving is real because the exact re-read touches only a handful of rows.

We already ship exactly this pattern at 392× the scale: `LagunaLmHeadPrune.swift:56–68` documents a three-level screen, `:816–828` builds the planes, `:938–985` is the decode path. Decode currently reads only the int5 `lo + scales` screen (109.8 MB) instead of the 411 MB BF16 LM-head plane, then refines exactly. **The router is the same problem at 1/392 the vocabulary.** `DARKBLOOM_LM_HEAD_PRUNE` is ON by default — read that code before you design anything.

## The correctness contract (VERIFIED THIS ROUND — read this twice)

`Sources/MLXFastModel/LagunaRuntimeLayers.swift:1387–1400`, `LagunaRuntimeMoEGate`, documented verbatim:

> *"Sigmoid top-k router. The routing math mirrors the vendored `LagunaMoEGate` exactly (sigmoid scores, **correction bias added only for expert CHOICE**, **mixture weights taken from the pre-bias scores**, optional top-k renormalization)."*

Fields: `topK`, `normTopkProb`, `routerLogitSoftcapping`, `@ParameterInfo weight`, `@ParameterInfo e_score_correction_bias`. Router dtype is asserted BF16 at `:2350`.

So your screen must reproduce **all** of the following exactly:

1. **The top-8 CHOICE under the bias-corrected scores** — including the exact tie-breaking behaviour of the current implementation. Two experts with equal corrected scores must resolve to the same winner as today.
2. **The mixture weights, which come from the PRE-bias sigmoid scores** of those 8 experts. This means a screen that only certifies *choice* is not enough — you also need the exact pre-bias score for the 8 winners.
3. `normTopkProb` renormalization over those 8 weights.
4. `routerLogitSoftcapping`, applied where the current code applies it.

Point 2 is the good news: **refining 8 rows exactly costs 8 × 2048 × 2 B = 32 KB per layer**, which is negligible against the 1,048,576 B you are trying to avoid. The design is therefore: *screen 256 experts cheaply, certify the top-8 boundary, then read 8 (plus any ambiguous) rows at full BF16 precision.*

## Target shapes

`LagunaRuntimeLayers.swift:1389–1396`. Per sparse layer (39 of 40 layers; layer 0 is dense):

- `weight`: `[256, 2048]` BF16 = **1,048,576 B**
- `e_score_correction_bias`: `f32[256]` = **1,024 B**

× 39 layers = **40,934,400 B/step**.

Savings arithmetic at the realised PR #110 price of **0.015224 % score per MB/step**:

| screen precision | screen bytes/step | saved | score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| INT8 | ~20.5 MB | **~20.4 MB** | **~0.31 %** |
| int5 (LM-head precedent) | ~12.8 MB | **~28.1 MB** | **~0.43 %** |
| int4 | ~10.2 MB | **~30.7 MB** | **~0.47 %** |

(All before adding back per-row scales and the exact re-read tail — compute the real net in Stage 1.)

## Stage 1 — the margin measurement (MANDATORY, decisive, cheap, no kernel)

**The 8th/9th margin distribution is the entire risk of this experiment.** If the corrected score gap between the 8th and 9th expert is routinely smaller than the quantization error bound, your screen degenerates into re-reading most of the 256 rows and the byte saving evaporates.

Measure it **before** building anything:

1. Instrument the existing router (research-only patch, not shipped) to dump, for each of the 39 sparse layers over a full 128-step decode pass, the sorted corrected scores and specifically the **margin `s[8th] − s[9th]`**.
2. For each candidate screen precision (INT8 / int5 / int4 with per-row or per-group scales), derive the **rigorous two-sided error bound** `ε` on a corrected score from the quantization scheme — an actual bound from the format, not an empirical spread.
3. Compute, per layer and pooled, the fraction of decode steps where `margin ≤ 2ε`, i.e. the fraction where the boundary is ambiguous and you must escalate to exact re-reads. Report the **distribution of the number of ambiguous experts per step**, not just the mean.
4. Compute the **net** bytes/step: screen plane + scales + 8 exact rows + ambiguous exact rows. Compare against 1,048,576 B/layer.

**Pre-register a go/no-go bar BEFORE you look at the data.** Suggested: proceed to Stage 2 only if the best precision achieves **≥ 40 % net byte reduction on the router family (≥ 16 MB/step saved, ≥ 0.24 % score)** with a **p99 ambiguous-expert count ≤ 16 per layer-step**. Write the bar into a preregistration commit, following `research/fern-r93-stage3-preregistration.md` as the template. If you want different numbers, argue for them in the preregistration — but fix them before reading the data.

**Stage 1 alone is a publishable terminal result either way.** A clean "the 8th/9th margin is too tight, here is the distribution, the family is closed" is worth as much to the programme as a win, and it costs a fraction of the effort.

## Stage 2 — build it (ONLY if Stage 1 clears the pre-registered bar)

Design sketch, adapt freely:

- Build the quantized screen plane at **runtime init** (not offline — the whole layout stack is built at runtime init, see `LagunaRuntimeModel.swift:9158–9204`). Follow the lane-major bank precedent in `LagunaRuntimeWeights.swift:866–878`.
- Keep the BF16 original resident and bound. It is read only by the exact-refine path. This is exactly what the QKV/o_proj lane-major banks already do: the stock scale plane stays bound but is read **only** under the escape condition.

items.title: fix(tweety): 7a SAF attacks no-op bug (getAttacks().add defensive copy) + doc-honesty
items.body:
## Defect (code bug + fabrication)

Cell 22 of `Tweety-7a-Extended-Frameworks.ipynb` (Social Argumentation Framework / ISS semantics) had a **code bug**: it added attacks via
```python
attacks_collection = saf.getAttacks()
attacks_collection.add(attack_ab); attacks_collection.add(attack_bc)
attacks_collection.add(attack_cb); attacks_collection.add(attack_cd)
```
but `SocialAbstractArgumentationFramework.getAttacks()` returns a **defensive copy**, so the `.add()` calls were a **no-op**. The committed output proved it — the framework printed:
```
<{A(+3-1),B(+2-0),C(+2-5),D(+2-1)},[]>
```
i.e. **zero attacks** despite the log line `Attaques ajoutees avec succes`. ISS therefore ran on a framework with no attacks (no propagation), and cell 23's interpretation then **fabricated** attack relations that did not exist (`B est attaque par A ... reste a 0.995`).

This was surfaced by po-2025's Tweety scan (c.631 follow-up, HAUT, "autres lanes OK"). G.1 firsthand-verified and found it **richer than reported**: the bug is in the CODE, not just the markdown.

## Fix

**Cell 22 code** — use `saf.addAttack(attacker, attacked)` directly (the DungTheory pattern used everywhere else in the repo, e.g. EAF/Reaf cells). Attacks now propagate into the framework.

**Cell 22 re-executed** via `nbconvert --execute` (Tweety 1.29 JVM + JDK17 portable, rule F satisfied). Authentic output:
```
Framework Social (SAF) cree:
<{A(+3-1),B(+2-0),C(+2-5),D(+2-1)},[(B,C), (C,B), (A,B), (C,D)]>   <- 4 attacks (was [])
Modele ISS (scores d'acceptabilite):
{A=0.748, B=0.193, C=0.230, D=0.511}                                     <- was 0.748/0.995/0.285/0.664
```
Interpretation of the corrected scores:
- **B collapses (0.995 -> 0.193)** because it is attacked by A (0.748) **and** C (0.230) — the double attack from a strong attacker is exactly the propagation ISS is meant to model.
- **A stays high (0.748)**: A is unattacked, so its score depends only on its own votes (+2).
- **D moderates (0.511)**: attacked only by weak C (0.230).

**Cell 23 markdown** — table + graph analysis rewritten to match the corrected scores and the real attack graph `A->B, B->C, C->B, C->D`. Stop & Repair respected (re-executed source, no hand-edited output).

## Verification

- **Re-exec**: whole-notebook `nbconvert --execute`, **0 errors** across all 37 cells.
- **Surgical splice (C.3)**: only cell 22 (source+outputs) and cell 23 (markdown) differ from `origin/main`; **11 other code cells restored byte-identical** (no timestamp churn from the full re-exec). Verified per-cell: `output-diff cells = [22]`, `source-diff cells = [22, 23]`.
- **Stop & Repair**: output is the authentic re-exec result, not a hand-edit (rule 6 / H satisfied).
- **Line endings**: LF preserved (0 CRLF). JSON valid.
- **Scope note**: `SocialAbstractArgumentationFramework` is the unique class with a defensive-copy `getAttacks()`; cell 31 (NAF) correctly shows its 4 attacks `[(c,b),(e,d),(b,a),(f,e)]` via the same `getAttacks().add()` pattern (its `getAttacks()` returns the live collection). So the fix is correctly scoped to the SAF cell.


Add Section 8 perceived-sharpness metrics and reorganize subsection o…rder

Deconvolution/AI sharpening barely moves the existing Section 8 metrics because they all reduce to a median nebula/background ratio, which washes out the sharp-edge tail and cancels same-image noise/signal scaling. ## Why

Phương's progress reached the instructor as a summary that could also be silently erased. Reading the live Firebase room showed the shared node holding **0/29 lessons, 0.4 hours, and two stale page views from Aug 4 — yet rewritten that same day**. That's the signature of an empty snapshot overwriting real work.

## Three problems, fixed

**1. Any device on the default `learner` role overwrote the shared node.**
`role` defaults to `learner` for every fresh browser, and `publishSnapshot` did a plain `set()` with no ownership check. Now guarded three ways: a browser that has ever been switched to Chính never publishes again (`services/deviceIdentity.ts`, wired into `setRole`), a completely empty snapshot is never published, and a device that doesn't own the node may only take it over with an at-least-as-complete snapshot.

The payload now carries exam attempts with every answer, assignment submission text, and notes. Publishing moved out of the Study Mode overlay into `AppShell` so it runs on every page.

**3. Grading was local-only.**
`setOverride` could only touch attempts made in the instructor's own browser. New `/review` console (sidebar entry visible only as Chính) renders each exam question with her answer and the expected one; overrides publish to `rooms/<room>/review/exams/<moduleId>` and her device adopts them via `useReviewReceiver`, so the corrected score reaches her.

- The previously-uncommitted cloud replica behind `services/cloudSync` — per-identity buckets, last-write-wins per key, reads stay local so the app still boots offline.

items.title: Fix: gate detection scores by the presence token
items.body:
First of all, thank you for `sam3-deploy` — your implementation was an invaluable reference for getting SAM3 running on DeepStream, and this is only a small refinement on top of your work. 🙏

## What

Gate the exported detection score by SAM3's **presence token**.

## Why

`Head.forward` used `scores = pred_logits.sigmoid()` only, dropping the scene-level presence gate that SAM3 applies:

```
final_scores = pred_logits.sigmoid() * presence_logits.sigmoid()   # HF transformers
```

Without it, concepts that are **absent** from a scene leak as high-confidence false positives — e.g. `human face` fires at **0.575** on a bus windshield in the exported model, whereas the reference HF `Sam3Model` produces nothing there. Verified on the **exported ONNX at fp32** (rules out TRT/fp16): the false positive disappears after the fix, and concepts that are present (license plates) are unchanged and match the reference.

Fixes #1.

## Change

- `_Decoder._decode` also returns `dec.presence_logits[-1]`.
- `_Decoder.forward` / `Sam3Wrapper.Head.forward` unpack and apply it:
  ```python
  scores = (pred_logits.sigmoid() * presence.sigmoid()).unsqueeze(-1)
  ```

Minimal and self-contained — no change to `--mask 0/1` output shapes or to the DeepStream parser (`nvdsparsebbox_sam3.cpp` / `libnvdsinfer_sam3.so`), since the corrected score is still written into `detections[..., 4]`.

## Summary
Two related changes: (1) fix a fan-out in the `behavior_scores` extraction that inflated `numerator`/`denominator` ~100–300×, and (2) enable the 12 new sentiment behaviors end-to-end.

### 1. Fan-out fix
`behavior_scores.sql` built its spine from `expert_performance_metrics` (epm) and `LEFT JOIN`ed the observe scores on `(expert_id, date)`. **epm is a tall per-metric table** (one row per expert/date/metric), so the row-level join multiplied every behavior by that expert's metric-count for the day.

- `calc`/rates are **unchanged** (the fan-out preserved ratios); only absolute volumes are corrected. Scoring was correct-by-accident before (engine scores on `calc`, and confidence's denom floor saturated regardless).

items.title: eval-app: offer N/A in annotation picker for any judge-null dimension
items.body:
## What & why

Follow-up to #589. While analyzing judge-vs-human disagreements in the unit-test `.ann.json` files, **46 of 47 "null" disagreements were `judge=null → human=3`**, and the human comments literally say *"No N/A option in the CRUD UI."* The judge was **correct** (per each rubric's N/A criterion) — the reviewer was forced to enter `3` because the picker had no way to *agree* with N/A. That's a UI gap manufacturing false disagreements, not judge miscalibration (which #589 handles).

**Root cause** — `eval/app/app/results/[...id]/page.tsx`:
```ts
const allowNa = dim.source === 'base' && NULLABLE_BASE_DIMENSIONS.has(dim.name);
```
The N/A button was offered **only** for the nullable *base* dimension (Tool Arguments). When the judge legitimately scored a **rubric** dimension `null` — e.g. `check-warnings`' *Actionability* / *Severity classification*, whose rubric says *"N/A when the project is clean"* — the picker showed only 1/2/3, forcing the reviewer to pick `3`.

## Fix

Extract the predicate into a pure, tested helper and enable N/A whenever the judge scored the dimension `null` (any source), in addition to the existing nullable-base case:

```ts
export function dimensionAllowsNa(source, name, judgeScore): boolean {
  return judgeScore === null
      || (source === 'base' && NULLABLE_BASE_DIMENSIONS.has(name));
}
```

The **"Agree All"** button and the row default already copy the judge's `null` through correctly (`corrected_score: … ?? d.score`); this only fixes the **manual per-row** review path.

**No schema/save changes needed** — `ann.schema.json` and the save-path zod schema already accept `corrected_score: null`, and `compare.ts` already excludes null from weighted means.

## Changes

- `eval/app/lib/types.ts` — new pure, exported `dimensionAllowsNa` helper.
- `eval/app/app/results/[...id]/page.tsx` — use it; swap the import; generalize the `allowNa` doc comment.
- `docs/specs/eval-crud-ui-spec.md` — document the generalized N/A rule.
- `eval/app/tests/unit/dimensionAllowsNa.test.ts` — cover both enable reasons + the negative cases.

- ✅ `npm run typecheck` clean
- ✅ `eslint` clean

Existing committed `.ann.json` files that already recorded `null → 3` won't retroactively change; on their next re-annotation the reviewer can now record `null → null`. items.title: Token usage ticker, accurate cost accounting, and a corrected keyword opportunity score (v0.13.0)
items.body:
Tokens were already captured on every provider call and written to `ailinking_spend_log`. They were simply never shown. This surfaces them, corrects a cost bug found while doing so, and fixes an opportunity score that was working against its own intent.

## 1. Token visibility

- **New `Providers/UsageStats`** is the read model over the spend log: per-run deltas, per-key totals, month and all-time rollups, and a provider/model/operation breakdown. Chat and embedding are never merged, since their cost profiles differ by orders of magnitude.
- **Live ticker** under the progress bar during a suggestion scan and an embedding build. The baseline is the spend-log high-water mark taken when the job starts, stored in the progress record rather than the browser, so the counter survives pause, resume and page reloads. Ticker text is composed server-side so it stays translatable.
- **AI Keys table** gains per-key monthly token columns, and a new **Token usage** card shows this month and all time side by side plus the model breakdown.
- Jobs that never call a provider (indexing) report no usage and the ticker stays hidden, so the zero-key path looks exactly as it did.

## 2. Cost accuracy (bug)

`Pricing::cents()` did `(int) ceil($cost)` where `$cost` was **already denominated in cents**. A typical 2,400-token request costing about 0.04c was recorded as a full cent: over 20x high. With a few hundred calls per scan that also tripped the monthly spend cap at a small fraction of real spend.

- Added `Pricing::cents_float()`. The log now stores full precision in `est_cost`, a column that was always `decimal(12,6)` and never used as such.
- `monthly_spend_cents()` now sums the log instead of the per-key integer counter. The cap still ceils when deciding, so it can never under-enforce.
- Added `KEY created (created_at)` to `spend_log`: the cap aggregates by date on every provider call, and the existing composite indexes `(provider, created_at)` / `(key_id, created_at)` cannot serve a bare date filter. `DB_VERSION` 1.2.0 to 1.3.0 so `dbDelta` adds it on upgrade.

## 3. Corrected opportunity score

The old score was `impressions × (21 − min(20, position)) / 20`, which peaks at **position 1**. A keyword already ranking first scored highest and consumed the link budget, even though that page needs another internal link least. It also fought the `+0.20` striking-distance bonus it was paired with, because the `+0.28` opportunity term could outvote it.

It is now expected click gain:

```
gain  = ctr(top 3) − ctr(current position), floored at 0   # positions 1-3 score nothing
reach = 1 up to position 20, then 20 / position            # one link will not lift page 5 to the top 3
opportunity = impressions × gain × reach
```

The curve now peaks inside the striking band instead of at the top of it, so it reinforces `is_striking()` rather than fighting it.

**Upgrade note:** existing keyword rows keep their old scores until you re-fetch from Search Console or re-import your CSV, which recomputes them. Called out in the changelog.

## Tests

New `tests/run-unit.php`, 46 assertions over the pure decision functions: the CTR curve, opportunity shape and decay, striking bounds, keyword relevance, naturalness, the `Pricing` rounding contract, and usage formatting. It includes an explicit regression that a striking-distance keyword must outrank one already at position 1, and an assertion that a typical request really does cost under a cent, which is what `ceil()` was hiding.

These live in the repository on purpose: the previous harness lived in `%TEMP%\ailtest` and has already been deleted by temp cleanup. They are excluded from the release zip, which is built from the plugin subtree only (verified).

items.body:
Closes #129.

## What moved

`scripts/apron.ts` §12-19 — docks, wardens, sieges, crossings, plunges, scores — built their worlds on FLAT. `apronTerrain` returns a featureless terrain unchanged, and FLAT has no features, so every one of those sections measured an apron with **no berm, no lip ring and no plate rings** on it, while the world still reported an apron and the docks still went on the plates.

Those sections now build on DUNES through a `playedGround()` helper that throws if it is ever handed a featureless terrain, or if `apronTerrain` declines to compose the ring. The mistake cannot be made silently again.

**The corrected score figure is 33%** of the same dunes lot without an apron, at 13.5 hauler plunges a match — printed in §17 so the 82% cannot be cited by accident. Spec 0003 and ADR 0026 both quoted 82% and an estimated 38%; both are updated and marked resolved.

## What it found

Moving to the dunes surfaced a real gameplay defect flat had been hiding. §19's `sum(unforced) === 0` reads **107 unforced warden departures over six matches, all 107 into the void** — every one of them a warden already airborne when its own plate ran out, thrown by `tryTerrainLaunch` off the plate ring's convex outer half a median 11.9 units inboard of the `wardenMargin` line of 6.

Fixing that means moving `wardenMargin`, `patrolRadius` or the ring, which is a gameplay change this ticket's acceptance criteria forbid. So §19 prints the figure as a tracked `defect()` against #153 rather than as a check: it does not count toward the exit code, and restoring it to a `check` is #153's acceptance criterion. Re-deriving `=== 0` up to `<= 107` was the alternative, and it turns a claim into a budget.

## Notes for review

- Thresholds in the moved sections were re-derived from dunes measurements, not carried over. §18's crossing ceilings went 8 → 6 and 15 → 8 (measured 3.1 a bank, worst 4.2) and its banker floor 9 → 11; §18's crossing counter itself had to change, because the old `rampId === null` filter counted 0-1 a match once the lip ring throws the hauler before the lip.
- `scripts/_probe.ts` is deleted. It is a self-declared throwaway ("delete this file before the feature lands"), referenced by nothing and in no package script. The commit that removed it said it touched nothing outside `apron.ts`, which was wrong; the deletion itself is right.
- §30's `LANDING = 8` cited a flat measurement. The constant is kept as a band ceiling, the citation is corrected to the dunes figure of 1.4.

## Verification

`pnpm test` exits 0 — the full fast gate, static plus sim. `tsx scripts/apron.ts` exits 0 at 332 ok and 1 tracked defect. §27, which two earlier iterations called a pre-existing failure blocking the gate, passes here.

items.title: Let the browser hold a page it already has
items.body:
Every route renders per request, and Next's default for that is
`private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate` — the right
answer for a page that might be personalised, and the wrong one here.
Nothing on this site is behind a login, no response varies by who is
asking, and the data underneath changes once a night at 6am. The cost was
paid on every tap: a round trip to the container before anything on
screen moved, which is what `app/loading.tsx`, `usePendingNav` and the
optimistic state in `Controls.tsx` are all there to cover for.

Route-level ISR can't do this. Eight of the nine routes read their
level/season from `searchParams` and so render per request whatever they
declare; `/games/[id]` is the one that doesn't, and it keeps
`force-dynamic` because the single thing ISR would freeze into its HTML
is the demo-or-live decision that the 30-second probe in `lib/cache.ts`
exists to keep current. So the window goes on the response instead: a
minute for the current season, five for the archive, with
`stale-while-revalidate` behind each so the held copy paints while the
refresh runs. Both are minutes rather than the hour `lib/cache.ts` holds,
because `/api/revalidate` can clear the server's cache and cannot reach a
browser — and a reload, the reflex of anyone waiting on a corrected
score, ignores both windows anyway.

Dropping `no-store` also gets the back button back: Chrome won't put a
`no-store` page in the bfcache, so backing out of a box score was
re-rendering it rather than restoring the scroll position it was left at.

The same `headers()` block gives the three PWA icons a week. Everything
Next content-hashes under `/_next/static` already goes out `immutable`
for a year; these are read straight from `public/`, which Next can't hash
and so won't assume anything about, and they were revalidating on every
launch — exactly when a phone in a stadium may have no network.

Verified against the production standalone build: the nine routes and
both their HTML and flight responses carry the new windows, `Vary: RSC,
Next-Router-State-Tree, Next-Router-Prefetch` is intact on both so no
cache can hand one to a request that asked for the other, the icons
report a week, and `/api/revalidate` and the rest of `public/` are
untouched.

Closes #48
Closes #49

items.title: Record the ECR-0084 candidate: current_severity_score has no reader
items.body:
## What changed

Appends a self-contained finding to `SPEC_AUTHOR_NOTES.md` — the canonical copy claude.ai can be handed, since it has the archive but not the repo.

## The finding

**ECR-0063 shipped `current_severity_score` so that "escalation becomes visible." Nothing reads it.** Every reference in the repo is persistence, schema, the field itself, or a conformance test asserting the column holds the right number. Zero consumers outside `findings/` — and `reporting/`, the one surface a person reads, never mentions it.

Demonstrated on the real stores:

```
finding A: severity_score=30.0   current_severity_score=88.0

ranking returned by FindingStore.query:
   B   ranks on 60.0   (current = 60.0)
   A   ranks on 30.0   (current = 88.0)     <- the most severe finding, ranked last
```

Both backends order on the frozen key (`postgres.py:353`, `memory.py:152`), the ECR-0062 cursor encodes it, and `ix_finding_status_sev` indexes it.

**Same family as ECR-0062**, mirrored: that found a field *accepted and ignored*; this is one *maintained and unread*.

## Why now

`current_severity_score` is exactly where a corrected score lands for a finding raised **before** the EA-0024 repair. So the repair that just put the KEV-confirmed vulnerability at rank 1 of 10,173 does not reach findings already raised.

**Latent, not live** — P-001 builds findings in-memory per run, so every finding today is a first raise and `current == severity`. Recorded as a record for the first deployment, per the C-041 precedent.

## The decision it needs

ECR-0063's reasoning still holds — `severity_score` must stay write-once because the ECR-0062 cursor keys on it — so "just order by the current score" is not available without reopening C-037's cleared hazard. The narrower question is what the field is *for*, with three shapes costed. My recommendation is that a surface read it first (cheapest, honest, answers ECR-0063's stated goal); whether escalation should *re-rank* is a separate owner decision that should not be smuggled in as an implementation detail.

Docs only.

items.body:
## What this amendment delivers

Records the methodologically significant correction to the H3a primary verdict.

A scoring-extractor bug (fixed in PR #19, commit f175e8d) systematically undercounted correct answers in chain-of-thought responses. Re-scoring with the corrected extractor flips the verdict on the parent pre-registration's primary hypothesis from **REFUTATION** to **INCONCLUSIVE**.

## Corrected verdict

| | Before fix (refuted) | After fix (inconclusive) |
|---|---|---|
| Parent β₂ (between-subjects) | +0.0021 (p=0.676) | **-0.0061 (p=0.096)** |
| Parent β₂ (within-subjects) | -0.0009 (p=0.427) | **-0.0029 (p=0.266)** |
| Per-item fixed-effects β₂ | -0.0016 (p=0.395) | **-0.0079 (p=0.133)** |

β₂ is now negative across all five fits in the sensitivity chain (4 of 5 with the arousal-magnitude on between-subjects as the lone positive). None reach Holm-corrected significance at α = 0.05 within the parent's primary hypothesis family. The hypothesis is supported in direction but not in magnitude at the pre-registered n.

## Per-level pattern (rescored)

The level-4 (Neutral) peak the parent predicted is the highest value in the rescored between-subjects curve (0.738). Level 7 (Strong negative) drops 16pp to 0.582 — substantial but not enough for a clean quadratic.

## Methodology trail

- Parent pre-registration: \`prereg-h3a-2026-04-27\` at 309e03b
- Bank expansion: \`prereg-h3a-amendment-001\` at fa609ba
- Within-subjects + arousal-magnitude sensitivity: \`prereg-h3a-amendment-002\` at c1e627c

Original on-disk corpora preserved as-collected; rescored copies at:

- \`results/h3a_2026-04-27_n122_rescored/\` (854 cells, between-subjects)
- \`results/h3a_2026-04-27_n122_within_subjects_rescored/\` (854 cells, within-subjects)

items.title: Narrow sparse hidden-bishop mate over-scoring that caused 2026-07-04 non-close miss
items.body:
The benchmark regression came from over-scoring an ultra-sparse checkmate as Medium when community outcomes clearly place it in Basic. The scorer lacked an ease rule for sparse “hidden bishop + hidden kings” geometry that is mechanically constrained despite tactical appearance.

- **Add narrowly-gated ease motif in `difficulty.js`**
  - Introduced `sparseHiddenBishopMateEase` in `extractDifficultyFeatures` for positions matching all of:
    - very low material (`totalPieces <= 6`)
    - mated king hidden + both kings hidden
    - hidden checking line present
    - hidden bishop present
    - no hidden queen/rook/knight/pawn
    - low attacker fan-out (`mateNetAttackers <= 3`)

- **Wire motif into calibration/scoring**
  - Added `sparseHiddenBishopMateEaseWeight: -14` to `DEFAULT_CALIBRATION`
  - Included the feature in additive contribution calculation
  - Exposed the flag in `details` for benchmark/debug introspection

- **Benchmark output update**
  - Regenerated benchmark section in `README.md` to reflect corrected scoring on 2026-07-04

```js
const sparseHiddenBishopMateEase =
  totalPieces <= 6 &&
  matedKingHidden &&
  bothKingsHidden &&
  hiddenCheckers >= 1 &&
  (hiddenPieceCounts.b ?? 0) >= 1 &&
  (hiddenPieceCounts.q ?? 0) === 0 &&
  (hiddenPieceCounts.r ?? 0) === 0 &&
  (hiddenPieceCounts.n ?? 0) === 0 &&
  (hiddenPieceCounts.p ?? 0) === 0 &&
  mateNetAttackers <= 3
    ? 1
    : 0;
```
